value.overview: The Red-crowned Parrot (Amazona viridigenalis) is a parrot recorded in the United States. Field recognition often comes from green body, red forehead and lores, blue crown tones, yellowish cheek area, and loud parrot flight calls. In the U.S. source data, it appeared in 3 state or DC summaries, including CA, HI, TX. It is most associated with Forests:  Tropical Dry, and local season should be checked before trip planning.
value.classification: The Red-crowned Parrot belongs to the family New World and African Parrots in the order Psittaciformes. This is the practical birding classification used for the BirdIntel profile cache.
value.identification: Look for green body, red forehead and lores, blue crown tones, yellowish cheek area, and loud parrot flight calls. Also use size, posture, flight style, voice, behavior, habitat, and season. Plumage can vary by sex, age, molt, and light, so the safest identification comes from combining several field marks rather than relying on one color or feature.
value.rangeHabitat: In the United States, this taxon was found in 3 state or DC summary files: CA, HI, TX. It is most often linked with Forests:  Tropical Dry. The exact range can be local, seasonal, or patchy, so recent sightings are still important for route planning and local birding decisions.
value.migrationStatus: In the United States, it can be resident in suitable parts of its range, although local movement may occur with food, weather, or water conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding typically uses tree cavities, palm cavities, or other enclosed sites where available. Pairs are strongly bonded, and both adults help feed the young. Large trees, safe nesting cavities, and reliable food supplies are important.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds on seeds, fruit, berries, blossoms, buds, and other plant material. Flocks often travel between feeding trees and roosting areas and use the bill and feet together while handling food.
value.behavior: It is social and noisy, often moving in pairs or flocks. Strong flight, communal roosting, and loud contact calls make parrots easier to detect than to approach closely.
